Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits

Changye Li Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Zijian Zhang Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: NVIDIA    Muheng Li Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Yiduo Pang Affiliation:  Zhejiang University    Tingjun Wu Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Menghan Li Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Yitong Liu Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Hongkai Guo Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Mengchi Chen Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Chenyu He Affiliation:  Zhejiang University    Kaisheng Ma Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Wei Xu Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Song Han Affiliation: NVIDIA Affiliation:  MIT    Sihao Liu Affiliation: NVIDIA    Ligeng Zhu Affiliation: NVIDIA
Abstract

Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent’s reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another’s work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most kk experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.08.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.46.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.

Code: https://github.com/humanfia/hma

1 Introduction

LLM-based agents tackle machine learning engineering (MLE) through repeated experiments: writing training code, running it, and evaluating candidate solutions (Chan et al., 2025; Toledo et al., 2025; Karpathy, 2026). For long-horizon tasks, producing a working solution is only the beginning: the agent must keep finding ways to improve it. As further gains become harder to find, the agent is expected to spend more tokens reasoning about the limitations of the current solution and deciding the next action. In our experiment across six models, however, mean output tokens per response—a proxy for reasoning intensity—decline over time as score gains diminish (Figure 2). We refer to this phenomenon as long-horizon deceleration and analyze its implications for prior agent design.

Existing approaches often seek to sustain improvement through context engineering, supplying Markdown instructions, skills, and accumulated knowledge to guide an agent’s next steps (Zhu et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Karpathy, 2026; Rajasekaran et al., 2025). However, guidance that helps one model need not help its successor. For example, OpenAI recommends rewriting AGENTS.md, skills, and task prompts when upgrading models (Provencher, 2026), while Anthropic advises removing instructions for checks that newer models can already perform on their own (Anthropic, 2026c). As model capabilities improve, guidance that once compensated for their limitations can thus become redundant or counterproductive. We observe a related pattern in our comparison of three custom MLE harnesses—systems that manage a model’s tools, context, and execution loop (Zhu et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Nevertheless, our comparison shows that the relative benefits of specialized harnesses diminish or reverse as the base model improves, even under longer execution budgets (Table 2). We refer to this decline in relative performance as harness staleness, which indicates the limitations of custom harness design.

These limitations motivate workflow-level coordination across agent sessions, each defined as an agent’s execution from context initialization to termination. In MLE, code, trained models, and evaluated candidates persist in a shared workspace, allowing successive agents to build on prior work (Zhao et al., 2026; Young, 2025). This persistence enables complementary roles: the agent that discovers a useful candidate need not be the one best suited to refine it, and subsequent changes can provide a new starting point when the first agent returns. We therefore ask: Can structured alternation convert complementary agent capabilities into a consistent advantage over the best single agent under a matched budget?

To address this question, we represent alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP). We establish sufficient conditions and derive experiment-budget bounds under which alternation exceeds single-agent reference limits, and identify when fixed-kk interruption retains this advantage (Sections 3.1–3.3). Building on these results, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which coordinates two native agents—complete model—harness pairs using official harnesses—through a shared workspace (Figure 1). Each session is capped at kk experiments; after each handoff, the other agent continues with the shared work and a reset context. The workflow leaves each agent’s tools, context management, and execution loop unchanged (Bolin, 2026; Anthropic, 2026b), and provides no task-specific knowledge at initialization. Because coordination depends on completed experiments and persistent task artifacts, application to other iterative optimization tasks is a natural question. In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We identify single-agent limitations and show how HMA sustains exploration. We characterize long-horizon deceleration across six models and harness staleness across three custom MLE harnesses in Sections 2. In contrast, from the early to the late phase of execution, HMA retains 86.4% of its mean output tokens per response, compared with 60.7% for matched single-agent baselines, indicating more persistent exploration across sessions.

  • •

    Alternation and workflow design extend single-agent limits. Our CR-SMDP analysis establishes sufficient conditions and experiment-budget bounds for exceeding single-agent reference limits (Theorem 3.3), and characterizes when fixed-kk interruption preserves this advantage Theorem 3.5). Algorithm 1 instantiates these principles with context reset, alternating agents, and final review of candidates (Sections 3.1–3.4).

  • •

    HMA achieves state-of-the-art any-medal performance with cross-pair generality. On MLE-bench, HMA achieves a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest published open-source workflow by 8.0 points. Across the six heterogeneous agent-pair configurations, HMA improves the any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, with gains in every configuration (Sections 4.2). We also explore applicability beyond MLE-bench through a supplementary 48-hour kernel-optimization case study (Section 4.5).

2 Motivation: Limits of Single-Agent Exploration

In this section, we investigate two limitations of single-agent MLE workflows: diminishing exploration over extended execution and limited transfer of harness improvements across model versions. These observations motivate HMA, which coordinates alternating agents from different providers to extend exploration beyond the capabilities of an individual model–harness system.

Long-horizon deceleration.

We examine six single-session configurations under /goal mode. Figure 2 reports mean output tokens per response in a trailing 30-minute window, used as a proxy for the agent’s reasoning intensity. Across configurations, response length decreases by 29.8%–45.0% from hours 0–2 to hours 3–5. Together with the rapid saturation of prefix gains in Figure 3, this reveals diminishing returns from continued single-agent exploration; detailed measurement definitions and supporting statistics are given in Appendix D.1.

Harness staleness.

To counter diminishing single-agent exploration, existing harnesses introduce planning, review, and context engineering (Young, 2025; Rajasekaran et al., 2025). With task-specific cold-start knowledge disabled for fairness, our comparison of recent MLE harnesses (Zhu et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026) reveals harness staleness: their benefits relative to the official harness diminish as the backbone improves (Table 2). The stronger performance of the official harness is consistent with a possible benefit from model–harness alignment acquired during training. This motivates treating each agent as an integrated model–harness system and studying how agents from different providers collaborate through workflow-level coordination. We present detailed configurations and results in Appendix D.2.

3 Method

In this section, we formulate Humanize MLE Agents (HMA) as a context-reset semi-MDP (Section 3.1), derive conditions and experiment budgets for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits (Section 3.2), analyze fixed-kk interruption and empirical cap selection (Section 3.3), and present the complete HMA workflow (Section 3.4).

3.1 HMA Preliminaries

Workflow policy and task state.

A multi-agent workflow that alternates between agent sessions is governed by a fixed policy over options μ\mu (Sutton et al., 1999). Without loss of generality, we consider two agents, AA and BB, working on a shared task. The state x=(W,E,c(u))x=(W,E,c^{(u)}) comprises the shared workspace WW, retained result EE, and context c(u)c^{(u)} of the active agent u∈{A,B}u\in\{A,B\}. Session ii of the workflow, executed by agent uu, is modeled as an option oi(u)=(ℐi(u),πi(u),βi(u))o_{i}^{(u)}=(\mathcal{I}_{i}^{(u)},\pi_{i}^{(u)},\beta_{i}^{(u)}), with initiation set ℐi(u):={x:μ⁡(oi(u)∣x)>0}\mathcal{I}_{i}^{(u)}:=\{x:\mu(o_{i}^{(u)}\mid x)>0\}, internal policy πi(u)\pi_{i}^{(u)}, and termination rule βi(u)\beta_{i}^{(u)}. Termination creates an option boundary, where μ\mu selects the next option.

For a general MLE task, NN is the total experiment budget of the workflow; each primitive step completes one experiment and updates (W,E)(W,E) within an option. The initial state x0=(W0,E0,∅)∼ν0x_{0}=(W_{0},E_{0},\emptyset)\sim\nu_{0} is drawn from the task-state distribution ν0\nu_{0}, with workspace W0W_{0}, empty result E0E_{0}, and empty context. Let EnE_{n} be the result retained after nn experiments, with normalized quality q⁡(x):=q⁡(E)∈[0,1]q(x):=q(E)\in[0,1]. Expected quality and target-success probability are Perfμ⁡(N):=𝔼μ,ν0​q​(EN)\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu}(N):=\mathbb{E}_{\mu,\nu_{0}}q(E_{N}) and pμ​(N,τ):=Prμ,ν0⁡(q⁡(EN)≥τ)p_{\mu}(N;\tau):=\Pr\nolimits_{\mu,\nu_{0}}(q(E_{N})\geq\tau) for τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1].

The option kernel is P(u)​(x,x′):=Pr⁡(xi+1=x′∣xi=x,ui=u)P^{(u)}(x,x^{\prime}):=\Pr\nolimits(x_{i+1}=x^{\prime}\mid x_{i}=x,u_{i}=u). Qμ​(x,oi(u))=r¯(u)​(x)+∑x′P(u)​(x,x′)​Vμ​(x′),Vμ​(x)=∑uμ⁡(oi(u)∣x)​Qμ​(x,oi(u)).Q^{\mu}(x,o_{i}^{(u)})=\bar{r}^{(u)}(x)+\sum\nolimits_{x^{\prime}}P^{(u)}(x,x^{\prime})V^{\mu}(x^{\prime}),\quad V^{\mu}(x)=\sum\nolimits_{u}\mu(o_{i}^{(u)}\mid x)Q^{\mu}(x,o_{i}^{(u)}). (1)

Context-Reset SMDP.

The HMA workflow is formulated as a context-reset SMDP (CR-SMDP), whose option boundaries preserve (W,E)(W,E) and reset context to ∅\emptyset. For integer cap k≥1k\geq 1, remaining experiment budget tt, and natural duration Ti(u)​(xi)T_{i}^{(u)}(x_{i}) measured in experiments, option ii completes di(u)=min⁡{Ti(u)​(xi),k,t}d_{i}^{(u)}=\min\{T_{i}^{(u)}(x_{i}),k,t\} experiments before natural termination, fixed-kk interruption, or budget exhaustion. If Ti(u)​(xi)>kT_{i}^{(u)}(x_{i})>k almost surely and t≥kt\geq k, then βi(u)(ℓ)=𝟏{ℓ≥k}\beta_{i}^{(u)}(\ell)=\mathbf{1}_{\{\ell\geq k\}} and di=kd_{i}=k, where ℓ\ell counts completed experiments within the option. Further formulation details and early natural termination analysis appear in Appendix A.1.

3.3 Fixed-k Interruption and Empirical Choice

In this section, we study when fixed-kk interruption maintains the advantage in Theorem 3.3 and motivate short caps empirically. For the optimal initial agent u0u_{0}, a sufficient condition to exceed U∗U_{*} is

Telescoping the option-level Bellman recursion gives Perfμk⁡(N)−Perfμ∞⁡(N)=𝒜μk​(N)\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{k}}(N)-\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{\infty}}(N)=\mathcal{A}_{\mu_{k}}(N). Substitution proves the claim; see Appendix A.3. ∎

Corollary 3.6 (Upper bound on the required cap).

Suppose Δμ∞​(N)>0\Delta_{\mu_{\infty}}(N)>0 and interruption losses decay geometrically with kk, then some finite 1≤k≤k01\leq k\leq k_{0} satisfies Perfμk⁡(N)>U∗\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{k}}(N)>U_{*}.

Empirically selected cap range: k≤5k\leq 5.

Figure 3 compares six goal and five NTA configurations on n=75n=75 MLE-bench tasks (Chan et al., 2025). The prefix curves show that k=5k=5 preserves most observed gains with fewer within-option experiments, motivating candidate caps k≤5k\leq 5. Detailed analysis are presented in Appendix A.3; statistical and empirical details are provided in Appendix B.

3.4 HMA Workflow Overview

In this section, we describe the implementation of the HMA workflow, including alternating agent execution and final review, as summarized in Algorithm 1.

Agent Execution.

Algorithm 1 implements μk=(A,B,u0,k)\mu_{k}=(A,B,u_{0},k) from x0∼ν0x_{0}\sim\nu_{0}. Here tt is elapsed time, tend=ttotalt_{\mathrm{end}}=t_{\mathrm{total}} is the final deadline, and ts=tend−trevt_{\mathrm{s}}=t_{\mathrm{end}}-t_{\mathrm{rev}} ends exploration. Then xi,−1=xi,ℓx_{i,-1}=x_{i,\ell} and xi+1=f⁡(xi,−1)x_{i+1}=f(x_{i,-1}) reset context for agent u¯\bar{u}.

Final review.

The archive ℰ\mathcal{E} stores evaluated candidates and their authors in order; (E−1,u−1)(E_{-1},u_{-1}) is the latest pair. We reserve the final trevt_{\mathrm{rev}} for the other agent u¯−1\bar{u}_{-1} to review the archive and select E^←Review(u¯−1)​(ℰ,E−1,tend)\widehat{E}\leftarrow\textsc{Review}^{(\bar{u}_{-1})}(\mathcal{E},E_{-1},t_{\mathrm{end}}), with E−1E_{-1} as the fallback. This cross-agent check seeks agreement on the best archived candidate without test-set scores, approximating the result-retention objective of Assumption 3.1 at final selection.

4 Experiment

4.1 Experiment Setup

Implementation details.

We implement HMA on Humanize (Liu et al., 2026), following Algorithm 1 with GPT, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and Claude agents, each using their native harness and max reasoning effort. For MLE-bench, each task run uses one NVIDIA A10 GPU and a six-hour budget: agents alternate under k=5k=5, reset context at each handoff, and reserve the final 15 minutes for final review. Exact model–harness mappings, hardware, baseline configurations, and framework details are given in Appendix C.

Benchmark.

Our main evaluation uses MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2025), comprising 75 Kaggle competitions requiring agents to develop machine learning solutions. We report the percentage of tasks earning any medal (All) or a gold medal (Gold), supplemented by complexity-specific and leaderboard-based metrics in Table 2. Test-set scores are unavailable to agents and used only for offline evaluation. Section 4.5 supplements this evaluation with an exploratory application to kernel optimization.

4.2 Main Comparison

HMA outperforms single-agent and specialized workflow baselines.

Table 2 compares HMA with single agents using native harnesses, evaluated in our experiments, and specialized workflows using results reported in their original papers (Zhu et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). Opus-first HMA achieves 78.2% overall medals, exceeding our strongest single-agent baseline at 72.4% and the highest published workflow baseline at 70.2%. HMA and our single-agent baselines share a six-hour budget, whereas the published workflows use 12–24 hours. HMA achieves these gains without task-specific knowledge bases or additional prompt engineering, while retaining the agents’ existing internal harnesses.

HMA improves heterogeneous agent pairs across capability levels.

Across five model pairs with constituent medal rates of 54.2%–72.4%, all six HMA configurations improve overall medal rate over the stronger constituent, and Gold, Med+, and mean percentile over constituent averages. For Opus–GPT, both starting orders retain the advantage, reaching 78.2% and 73.3% medals versus the stronger constituent’s 72.4%, indicating that the observed advantage is not tied to a single favorable initial agent.

4.3 Experiment Analysis and Ablation Study

HMA sustains exploration and continued improvement.

The response-level curve in Figure 4 (a) uses the same 30-minute trailing window. From hours 0–2 to hours 3–5, HMA retains 86.4% of its mean output tokens per response, versus 60.7% for matched goal references. In Figure 4 (b), the six HMA configurations reach 42.7%–60.0% medals within two hours and continue improving through six hours, contrasting with the single-agent deceleration in Section 2.

Final review improves historical any-medal retention.

Holding exploration fixed, final review changes 8.9% of selections and increases any-medal outcomes from 311 to 319, with no losses relative to the pre-review candidate. Among the 450 task runs, 330 produce at least one medal-winning exploration candidate; final selection retains a medal in 319 of these runs (96.7%), compared with 311 (94.2%) before final review. These results quantify how terminal review supports the best-result retention objective in Assumption 3.1.

Additional analyses and ablations.

Appendix E details the weighting and aggregation used to construct the mean curves in Figure 4, together with trajectory construction and task-level comparisons. Appendix F further examines starting-order effects, model time allocation, and partner participation (Appendix F.1); the interruption-parameter ablations(Appendix F.2); natural termination and the fixed-duration approximation (Appendix F.3); and final review’s effects on final selection and historical any-medal retention (Appendix F.4).

4.4 Case Study

On INGV Volcanic Eruption Prediction, GPT and Opus improve the historical best MAE in five of six post-handoff options (Figure 5). Their final MAE of 34,234 is 46.5% below the best of six constituent goal runs. Mean response length also increases on four of five returns to a previously used model, illustrating continued refinement of shared task state alongside renewed output. Appendix G provides detailed measurements and additional cross-model cases.

4.5 Exploratory Application Beyond MLE-bench

The preceding case illustrates continued refinement within MLE. We next explore the workflow on Anthropic’s Original Performance Take-Home (AOPT) (Anthropic, 2026a), a kernel-optimization task measured in simulated execution cycles. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6-astra alternate with a cap of three accepted submissions per session (cap 3). The selected 48-hour run reaches 878 cycles at 34 hours 33 minutes and retains this score in its final candidate. Figure 6 pairs the performance trajectory with response-length traces, following the presentation in Figure 5.

For context, 878 cycles matches the 10th-ranked score on the Paradigm community leaderboard as of October 8, 2026 (Paradigm, 2026), just 14 cycles (1.62%) above the leading score of 864 cycles. The leaderboard uses a separate nine-seed judge, so this is a comparison of reported scores rather than a verified leaderboard placement. This single-run case provides preliminary evidence of the workflow’s applicability to kernel optimization beyond MLE-bench over a longer horizon.

5 Related Work

MLE agents and harness-level systems.

MLE-bench evaluates autonomous agents on Kaggle competitions (Chan et al., 2025). Recent MLE systems improve individual agents through search, reflection, memory, branch reuse, recoverable workspaces, or task-conditioned interfaces (Toledo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). These methods modify how one model acts within its harness. HMA instead leaves each native model–harness pair unchanged and coordinates complete agents at the workflow level.

Multi-agent and long-horizon workflows.

Prior workflows sustain long-horizon execution through reusable experience, reflection, tree search, workflow search, communication, role assignment, checkpointing, or independent review (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Recent handoff studies examine candidate transfer, learned control exchange, and the quality cost of continuing another model’s trajectory (Luo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Ganz et al., 2026). HMA studies fixed-cap alternation of complete native agents on one shared workspace, with a context reset at every handoff.

Options and semi-MDPs.

Semi-Markov decision processes model actions with variable duration, while options represent such actions through an internal policy and termination rule (Bradtke and Duff, 1994; Dietterich, 2000). The interruption theorem characterizes when terminating an option early preserves or improves continuation value (Sutton et al., 1999); subsequent work studies learned and off-policy termination (Bacon et al., 2017; Harutyunyan et al., 2018). HMA models each agent session as an option and applies this framework to fixed-cap alternation with context reset.

6 Conclusion

HMA alternates native agents, resetting context while preserving shared task state. Our CR-SMDP analysis gives sufficient conditions and budget bounds for exceeding single-agent reference limits and conditions for preserving this advantage under fixed-cap interruption. Across six MLE-bench configurations, HMA outperforms the stronger constituent in medal rate under equal six-hour budgets, reaching 78.2% at best. A supplementary AOPT case illustrates application to kernel optimization over 48 hours; establishing comparative gains beyond MLE-bench remains future work. Together, these results motivate further study of workflow-level coordination for sustained exploration across iterative optimization tasks.

Perfμk⁡(2​k​m)≥τ​pμk​(2​k​m,τ)≥τ⁡(1−Fm)≥τ⁡[1−F0​(1−a)m].\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{k}}(2km)\geq\tau p_{\mu_{k}}(2km;\tau)\geq\tau(1-F_{m})\geq\tau[1-F_{0}(1-a)^{m}]. (14)

Bounded monotone convergence ensures that UμkU_{\mu_{k}} exists; letting m→∞m\to\infty gives Uμk≥τ>U∗U_{\mu_{k}}\geq\tau>U_{*}. The same proof permits early natural termination when Assumption 3.2 holds for the resulting kernels, since Cμk,m≤2​k​mC_{\mu_{k},m}\leq 2km still holds. ∎

Corollary A.7 (Experiment budget; Corollary 3.4 restated).

Under the theorem’s conditions, let F0=1F_{0}=1 and fix p0∈(0,1)p_{0}\in(0,1). For 0<a≪10<a\ll 1, a sufficient budget for pμk​(N,τ)≥p0p_{\mu_{k}}(N;\tau)\geq p_{0} has the leading form

Nsuff​(k,p0,τ)=2​ka​log⁡11−p0​[1+O⁡(a)].N_{\mathrm{suff}}(k,p_{0},\tau)=\frac{2k}{a}\log\frac{1}{1-p_{0}}\,\bigl[1+O(a)\bigr]. (15)
Proof of Corollary A.7.

For 0<a<10<a<1, the bound pμk​(2​k​m,τ)≥1−(1−a)mp_{\mu_{k}}(2km;\tau)\geq 1-(1-a)^{m} reaches p0p_{0} once m≥log⁡(1/(1−p0))/[−log⁡(1−a)]m\geq\log(1/(1-p_{0}))/[-\log(1-a)]. Hence the exact rounded sufficient budget is

Using −log⁡(1−a)=a+O⁡(a2)-\log(1-a)=a+O(a^{2}) and a rounding error below 2​k2k gives (2​k/a)​log⁡(1/(1−p0))+O⁡(k)(2k/a)\log(1/(1-p_{0}))+O(k), equivalent to equation 15 for fixed p0p_{0}. Finally, p0=(U∗+η)/τp_{0}=(U_{*}+\eta)/\tau, 0<η<τ−U∗0<\eta<\tau-U_{*}, gives Perfμk⁡(N)≥U∗+η\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{k}}(N)\geq U_{*}+\eta by Proposition A.3. ∎

Startup and initial-agent effects.

Startup denotes the early cycles before cooperative progress stabilizes. The initial agent can affect access to GG and finite-budget quality. If the two starts later have similar conditional success rates, their subsequent budget scales 2​k/a2k/a are similar, while their startup progress can still differ.

A.3 Interruption Guarantee and Sufficient Caps

We expand Section 3.3. Corollary A.8 extends the alternation guarantee to NTA. We define interruption advantages in Definition A.9 and compare the workflows through option-level Bellman recursions. Theorem A.10 compares fixed-kk interruption with NTA; Corollaries A.11–A.12 give a finite candidate condition and the explicit cap bound underlying Corollary 3.6.

Corollary A.8 (Natural termination and quality limits).

For Natural-Termination Alternation (NTA), use μ∞=(A,B,u0,∞)\mu_{\infty}=(A,B,u_{0},\infty). Under Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 and almost-surely finite option durations, let Mτ:=inf{m≥0:q⁡(x2​m)≥τ}M_{\tau}:=\inf\{m\geq 0:q(x_{2m})\geq\tau\}. Then Cμ∞,Mτ<∞C_{\mu_{\infty},M_{\tau}}<\infty almost surely and Uμ∞≥τ>U∗U_{\mu_{\infty}}\geq\tau>U_{*}. If NTA and a finite cap satisfy access for every τ∈(U∗,U†)\tau\in(U_{*},U^{\dagger}), where U†∈(U∗,1]U^{\dagger}\in(U_{*},1] bounds both reachable quality spaces, then Uμk=Uμ∞=U†U_{\mu_{k}}=U_{\mu_{\infty}}=U^{\dagger}.

Proof of Corollary A.8.

Applying equation 12 to NTA gives Prμ∞⁡(Mτ>m)≤F0​(1−a)m→0\Pr\nolimits_{\mu_{\infty}}(M_{\tau}>m)\leq F_{0}(1-a)^{m}\to 0, with a=α​βa=\alpha\beta. Thus MτM_{\tau} and the sum of its option durations are almost surely finite. Monotone quality yields Uμ∞≥τU_{\mu_{\infty}}\geq\tau. Combining this argument with Theorem A.6 for every τ∈(U∗,U†)\tau\in(U_{*},U^{\dagger}) and using the common upper bound gives equality for both limits. ∎

Definition A.9 (Interruption advantage and reference margin).

Fix μk=(A,B,u0,k)\mu_{k}=(A,B,u_{0},k) and NN. The workflows μk\mu_{k} and μ∞=(A,B,u0,∞)\mu_{\infty}=(A,B,u_{0},\infty) share internal policies and boundary updates and differ only in option termination. Following Section 3.3, xi,0=xix_{i,0}=x_{i} is option ii’s entry, xi,−1=xi,di(ui)x_{i,-1}=x_{i,d_{i}^{(u_{i})}} its endpoint before reset, and xi+1,0=f⁡(xi,−1)x_{i+1,0}=f(x_{i,-1}) the next entry, with q⁡(xi+1,0)=q⁡(xi,−1)q(x_{i+1,0})=q(x_{i,-1}).

At an added cap interruption, NTA would continue from xi,−1x_{i,-1} with the current context. Ending the option instead gives advantage Aμ∞​(xi,−1):=Vμ∞​(xi+1,0)−Qμ∞​(xi,−1,oi(ui))A^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i,-1}):=V^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i+1,0})-Q^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i,-1},o_{i}^{(u_{i})}). Both values use NTA with the same remaining experiment budget; the next entry activates the other agent with empty context. The interruption contribution is zero at natural termination or budget exhaustion.

The added interruptions are indexed by

𝒥μk(N):={i≥0:∑j=0idj(uj)<N,di(ui)=k<Ti(ui)(xi,0)}.\mathcal{J}_{\mu_{k}}(N):=\left\{i\geq 0:\sum_{j=0}^{i}d_{j}^{(u_{j})}<N,\ d_{i}^{(u_{i})}=k<T_{i}^{(u_{i})}(x_{i,0})\right\}.

Thus natural termination takes precedence when it coincides with the cap. The expected net gain is 𝒜μk​(N):=𝔼μk​∑i∈𝒥μk​(N)Aμ∞​(xi,−1)\mathcal{A}_{\mu_{k}}(N):=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{\mu_{k}}(N)}A^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i,-1}), and the NTA margin is Δμ∞​(N):=Perfμ∞⁡(N)−U∗\Delta_{\mu_{\infty}}(N):=\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{\infty}}(N)-U_{*}.

Theorem A.10 (Expected advantage under fixed-k interruption; Theorem 3.5 restated).

For the selected initial agent u0u_{0}, a sufficient condition to exceed U∗U_{*} is

Δμ∞​(N)+𝒜μk​(N)>0⟹Perfμk⁡(N)>U∗.\Delta_{\mu_{\infty}}(N)+\mathcal{A}_{\mu_{k}}(N)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{k}}(N)>U_{*}. (17)
Proof of Theorem A.10.

Let MM be the number of options executed under μk\mu_{k} within budget NN, with xM,0x_{M,0} terminal, and let ιi:=𝟏{i∈𝒥μk(N)}\iota_{i}:=\mathbf{1}_{\{i\in\mathcal{J}_{\mu_{k}}(N)\}}. For each i<Mi<M, the option-level Bellman recursion (Sutton et al., 1999, proof of Theorem 2) gives

𝔼μk​[q⁡(xi+1,0)−q⁡(xi,0)+Vμ∞​(xi+1,0)∣xi,0]−Vμ∞​(xi,0)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\!\left[q(x_{i+1,0})-q(x_{i,0})+V^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i+1,0})\mid x_{i,0}\right]-V^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i,0}) (18)
=𝔼μk​[ιi​Aμ∞​(xi,−1)∣xi,0].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\!\left[\iota_{i}A^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i,-1})\mid x_{i,0}\right].

Since Vμ∞​(xM,0)=0V^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{M,0})=0 and x0,0=x0∼ν0x_{0,0}=x_{0}\sim\nu_{0}, summing telescopes:

=𝔼μk​∑i∈𝒥μk​(N)Aμ∞​(xi,−1)=𝒜μk​(N).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}_{\mu_{k}}(N)}A^{\mu_{\infty}}(x_{i,-1})=\mathcal{A}_{\mu_{k}}(N).

Thus Perfμk⁡(N)−U∗=Δμ∞​(N)+𝒜μk​(N)\operatorname{Perf}_{\mu_{k}}(N)-U_{*}=\Delta_{\mu_{\infty}}(N)+\mathcal{A}_{\mu_{k}}(N), which proves equation 17. ∎

Appendix B Prefix Retention and Empirical Cap Selection

We quantify the observed gains retained by short prefixes and provide the simultaneous confidence construction used to motivate candidate caps in Section 3.3. Executed fixed-kk outcomes are analyzed separately in Appendix F.

B.1 Retention Statistics and Confidence Bounds

We establish the statistical guarantee supporting Section 3.3. Definition B.1 specifies task-level prefix retention, Assumption B.2 states the sampling condition, and Proposition B.3 gives simultaneous 1−δ1-\delta lower confidence bounds.

Definition B.1 (Observed prefix gain).

For policy μ\mu and task jj, define

𝒪μ,j:={i:oi(ui)​ is recorded on task ​j​ under ​μ}.\mathcal{O}_{\mu,j}:=\{i:o_{i}^{(u_{i})}\text{ is recorded on task }j\text{ under }\mu\}.

For each session index i∈𝒪μ,ji\in\mathcal{O}_{\mu,j}, let lil_{i} be its recorded experiment count and qi​(d)q_{i}(d) its best quality after dd experiments, with entry quality at d=0d=0. For integer k≥0k\geq 0, define

gi​(k)=qi​(min⁡{k,li})−qi​(0),ζμ,j​(k)=∑i∈𝒪μ,jgi​(k)∑i∈𝒪μ,jgi​(li).g_{i}(k)=q_{i}(\min\{k,l_{i}\})-q_{i}(0),\qquad\zeta_{\mu,j}(k)=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{O}_{\mu,j}}g_{i}(k)}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{O}_{\mu,j}}g_{i}(l_{i})}. (22)

The ratio is defined for positive total gain; nμn_{\mu} counts these tasks.

Assumption B.2 (Independent task observations).

For each prespecified policy μ\mu, cap kk, and statistic, let Yj∈[0,1]Y_{j}\in[0,1] be ζμ,j​(k)\zeta_{\mu,j}(k) or 𝟏{ζμ,j(k)≥0.9}\mathbf{1}_{\{\zeta_{\mu,j}(k)\geq 0.9\}}. Conditional on defined ratios, assume independence across the nμn_{\mu} tasks. Dependence across configurations and caps is allowed.

Proposition B.3 (Simultaneous lower confidence bounds).

Under Assumption B.2, set Y¯=nμ−1​∑jYj\bar{Y}=n_{\mu}^{-1}\sum_{j}Y_{j} and μY=nμ−1​∑j𝔼​Yj\mu_{Y}=n_{\mu}^{-1}\sum_{j}\mathbb{E}Y_{j}. For McmpM_{\mathrm{cmp}} prespecified comparisons and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), define μ¯Y≤Y¯\underline{\mu}_{Y}\leq\bar{Y} by

nμdKL(Y¯∥μ¯Y)=log(Mcmp/δ),n_{\mu}d_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar{Y}\|\underline{\mu}_{Y})=\log(M_{\mathrm{cmp}}/\delta), (23)

with μ¯Y=0\underline{\mu}_{Y}=0 when Y¯=0\bar{Y}=0. Then Pr⁡(μ¯Y≤μY​ for all comparisons)≥1−δ\Pr(\underline{\mu}_{Y}\leq\mu_{Y}\text{ for all comparisons})\geq 1-\delta.

Proof of Proposition B.3.

The exponential-moment bound (Garivier and Cappé, 2011, Lemma 9), Jensen’s inequality, and Chernoff optimization give Pr(Y¯≥z)≤e−nμdKL(z∥μY)\Pr(\bar{Y}\geq z)\leq e^{-n_{\mu}d_{\mathrm{KL}}(z\|\mu_{Y})} for μY<z≤1\mu_{Y}<z\leq 1. Inverting at failure level δ/Mcmp\delta/M_{\mathrm{cmp}} gives equation 23; a union bound over the comparisons proves the claim. ∎

B.2 Configurations and Observed Prefix Results

This subsection documents the MLE-bench configurations and results supporting empirical cap selection in Section 3.3 and Figure 3.

Table 3 lists six goal and five NTA configurations, all using max reasoning effort. A goal task run is one continuous session; NTA alternates at natural termination, starting with the first listed model. Harness documentation is provided by Bolin (2026); Anthropic (2026b); Moonshot AI (2026); DeepSeek-AI (2026).

For MLE-bench, we use q=1−(position−1)/(leaderboard​size)q=1-(\mathrm{position}-1)/(\mathrm{leaderboard\ size}) on 75 tasks, including 75 measured Opus goal runs. Each goal task run is one option; NTA follows recorded boundaries, giving 1,065 options.

At each kk, Figure 3 plots the mean of min⁡{k,li}/li\min\{k,l_{i}\}/l_{i} across options horizontally and gain retention averaged across tasks within each configuration, then equally across configurations vertically, both as percentages. Individual curves use each configuration’s data, starting at (0,0)(0,0) and ending at (100,100)(100,100) at its maximum option length.

At k=1,3,5k=1,3,5, mean gain retention is 63.15%, 93.35%, and 97.83%, with experiment fractions 24.76%, 54.88%, and 73.77%. At k=5k=5, individual configurations retain 96.11%–99.20% (Opus: 98.74%), motivating candidates 1≤k≤51\leq k\leq 5.

For eleven configurations, fifty caps (k=1,…,50k=1,\ldots,50), and two statistics, Mcmp=1100M_{\mathrm{cmp}}=1100. At δ=0.05\delta=0.05 and k=5k=5, 87.84%–98.67% of tasks retain at least 90% of gains; Appendix B.1 gives simultaneous lower bounds of 65.08%–83.30%.

Appendix C Experimental Setup and Reproducibility

We collect the execution environment, agent configurations, baseline settings, evaluation rules, and repeat protocol used throughout the experiments. Empirical findings are separated into Appendices D–G.

C.1 Humanize and Execution Environment

Terminology.

A configuration specifies the agent or agent pair, starting order, cap, and budget. A task run is one complete execution on one task; a repeat evaluates the full task suite. Each agent session is modeled as an option, with experiments counted within it; a model response is one recorded output from a model call.

Framework.

We implement the workflow on Humanize (Liu et al., 2026), which coordinates agent execution in a shared workspace, fixed-kk interruption, and final review as specified in Algorithm 1. The model harness supplies the internal agent policy; the workflow controls option boundaries and preserves shared task workspace. HMA uses k=5k=5 and ttotal=21600t_{\mathrm{total}}=21600 seconds per task, including trev=900t_{\mathrm{rev}}=900 seconds reserved for the other agent’s final review. Thus exploration ends at ts=20700t_{\mathrm{s}}=20700 seconds.

Hardware.

Our execution environment exposes 30 vCPUs backed by an Intel Xeon Platinum 8358 processor, 220 GiB RAM, and one NVIDIA A10 GPU. The GPU reports 24 GiB of available device memory. These resources are shared by the two alternating agents within a single task run.

C.2 Agent and Baseline Configurations

Agents.

Table 4 lists the full model names and native harnesses. In analyses and figures, GPT, Kimi, GLM, and Opus abbreviate GPT-5.6-sol, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and Claude Opus 5; DeepSeek-V4 and DeepSeek-V4.1 abbreviate the corresponding Flash models. DeepSeek alone denotes the version specified for the configuration. All agents in our runs use max reasoning effort. Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, and DeepSeek Harness provide the model execution interfaces (DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Bolin, 2026; Anthropic, 2026b; Moonshot AI, 2026). Appendix B.2 separately lists the goal and NTA configurations used for prefix analysis.

Comparison baselines.

We include ScienceFlow, MLEvolve, and ML-Master 2.0 using their reported results (Zhao et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). Table 5 records their original configurations; the max reasoning setting applies to our runs, while these published results retain their reported inference settings.

C.3 Evaluation Protocol and Repeats

Evaluation metrics.

Lite, Medium, High, and All denote the 22-, 38-, 15-, and 75-task sets, respectively. Lite, Medium, and High report medal percentages within each complexity group; All reports the medal percentage over the full 75-task suite. For repeated evaluations, rates are calculated from per-repeat medal counts before averaging. Table 2 reports all performance metrics to one decimal place. Within a model pair, Avg. of Single averages the two constituent goal means with equal weight; HMA gains are computed against this mean before rounding. Gold is the percentage of tasks attaining a gold medal. Med+ is the percentage outperforming the human leaderboard median. Mean percentile averages the task-level leaderboard percentile over the evaluated suite, using the rank convention in Appendix B.2. All metrics use the workflow’s returned candidate; for HMA this is the final review selection or its fallback in Algorithm 1. Test-set scores are computed offline.

Repeated evaluations.

Each configuration is evaluated in three independent repeats over the fixed 75-task suite. Reported values average the three repeats; published baseline uncertainties retain their original definitions.

Appendix D Additional Evidence for the Motivation

We provide the detailed evidence behind the two motivation claims in Section 2: response-length decay in uninterrupted runs and harness staleness across model versions.

D.1 Declining Response Length in Single-Agent Runs

Configurations.

We document Figure 2 using the six configurations in Table 4. The /goal protocol runs one agent until natural termination or exhaustion of six hours of active runtime, without model alternation or fixed-cap interruption. Each of the six configurations is evaluated on 75 tasks with three independent repeats and max reasoning effort. Recorded cohorts and prompt policies are retained.

Response-level moving average.

Figure 2 reports mean output tokens per recorded model response. At one-minute active-runtime checkpoints, we divide the sum of provider-reported output tokens by the number of responses in the preceding 30 minutes, pooling the 75 tasks and repeats within each configuration. Near the origin, the window uses the elapsed prefix; windows without responses are undefined. This response-weighted statistic excludes tool-return text, input tokens, and coordinator output, while retaining model responses that request tools.

Early versus late responses.

Table 6 compares responses in hours 0–2 and 3–5 using raw event totals divided by response counts in each interval. All six configurations show a reduction of 29.8%–45.0%; these interval statistics are computed before temporal smoothing.

D.2 Harness Staleness across Model Versions

Comparison setup.

We compare ML-Master 2.0 (Zhu et al., 2026), MLEvolve (Du et al., 2026), and ScienceFlow (Zhao et al., 2026) with the official DeepSeek Harness on a 16-task MLE-bench subset (Chan et al., 2025), using DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. We retain the research harnesses’ original workflow designs and experimental settings while disabling task-specific cold-start knowledge wherever present. Execution budgets are reported in Table 2. DeepSeek Harness runs each model under /goal with max reasoning effort for six hours; its reported medal rate is averaged over three repeats.

Result accounting.

Medal rates use all 16 tasks as the denominator. The disqualified ScienceFlow run on Chaii with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is counted as no medal because its checkpoint had seen the test answers. Table 2 reports medal rates and percentage-point differences from the corresponding DeepSeek Harness baseline. Table 7 provides the task-level outcomes. These 16-task DeepSeek Harness references are distinct from the full 75-task results in Table 2.

Appendix E Additional Main-Comparison Analyses

We supplement the main comparison with the aggregation rules, response and performance trajectories, matched constituent weighting, and task-level comparisons used for Figure 4.

Analysis configurations.

We analyze the five participating goal models and six HMA configurations in Table 2, using the protocol in Appendix C. The trajectory aggregation and matched constituent construction follow the definitions below. The separate scheduling ablations appear in Appendix F.

Performance and response trajectories.

At each active-runtime checkpoint, we aggregate the medal status of the latest accepted candidate on each task, assigning zero before a valid submission. Final points use the returned candidate under the recorded selection rule. Scores use the corrected answer keys. Receipt processing at the nominal deadline is included in the final point. Figure 4 (a) uses the response-level statistic in Appendix D.1: at each one-minute checkpoint, total actor output tokens in the preceding 30-minute trailing window are divided by the number of recorded responses, pooling tasks and repeats within each configuration and including HMA’s final review. Near the origin, the window uses the elapsed prefix; empty windows are undefined. Figure 4 (b) retains the unsmoothed medal-rate trajectory. Token counts measure output volume across different tokenizers, not a common monetary or computational cost. Neither panel extrapolates trajectories or uses best-so-far score selection.

Matched group-average curves.

Figure 4 assigns weight 1/61/6 to each HMA configuration. For configuration jj with constituent models Aj,BjA_{j},B_{j}, its goal reference is (YAjgoal​(t)+YBjgoal​(t))/2(Y_{A_{j}}^{\mathrm{goal}}(t)+Y_{B_{j}}^{\mathrm{goal}}(t))/2, where YY denotes mean output tokens per response or medal rate, computed within each configuration as above. We average these six references at each common runtime checkpoint. The resulting matched model weights are reported in Table 9; the same weights are used for Goal and HMA, so each model contributes equally to both references. DeepSeek-V4-Flash is excluded because it appears in none of the six HMA configurations. This matches the mean-of-constituents reference used for the gains in Table 2; the weights describe configuration composition rather than measured execution-time shares. Both panels use active runtime horizontally, with mean output tokens per response in (a) computed over a 30-minute trailing window and mean medal rate in (b). Faint curves retain the participating configurations. For the early/late comparison, we divide raw output-token totals by response counts separately in hours 0–2 and 3–5 within each configuration, then apply the same group weights. The resulting means are 610.9 and 527.6 tokens per response for HMA, and 650.3 and 394.9 for goal, retaining 86.4% and 60.7%, respectively; these interval statistics are computed before temporal smoothing.

Early progress and task-level gains.

Table 9 reports the any-medal rates at two hours and at the six-hour endpoint. The six HMA configurations attain 57.3%, 58.7%, 54.7%, 60.0%, 50.7%, and 42.7% medals at two hours, with corresponding final rates of 78.2%, 73.3%, 72.0%, 70.7%, 69.3%, and 62.7%. Across matched GPT goal comparisons, GPT–Kimi HMA gains medals on 5, 4, and 6 tasks and loses them on 4, 3, and 2, yielding net gains of 1, 1, and 4. These successful tasks remain within the evaluated goal-task union, characterizing gains achieved within the six-hour budget.

Appendix F Ablation Studies

We supplement Section 4.3 with starting-order effects, executed fixed-kk comparisons, natural-termination statistics, and a selection-only final review audit. We discuss order before cap size because model exposure within a finite time budget depends on both.

F.1 Starting-Order Effects

We compare GPT-first and Kimi-first alternation under NTA and HMA with k=5k=5, then relate the endpoint differences to model-session time and partner participation.

Configurations.

Each configuration covers the same 75 tasks with a six-hour budget and max reasoning effort. The additional Kimi-first HMA run records 283 exploration options: among the 75 initial options, 52 reach the cap, 22 end naturally, and one reaches the deadline. The GPT-first k=5k=5 run records 277 exploration options, with 66 initial cap closures and nine natural exits. Corrected answer keys give 42/75 medals for Kimi-first NTA, including three corrected outcomes. For the Kimi-first HMA archive, the terminal window is 21,700 seconds; all accepted candidates arrive within 21,600 seconds and its six-hour medal count matches the returned result.

Final quality and finite-budget exposure.

Figure 7(a) compares both GPT–Kimi starting orders under the six-hour budget. NTA reaches 77.3% and 56.0% medals with GPT and Kimi first, respectively; HMA with k=5k=5 reaches 70.7% and 66.7%, narrowing the observed gap from 21.3 to 4.0 percentage points. The six-hour horizon limits sustained participation by both agents under NTA: by 5.75 hours, the second agent has produced a recorded response on only 19/75 GPT-first tasks and 47/75 Kimi-first tasks. Under NTA, the nominal first model occupies about 81–83% of the budget. Because the GPT goal baseline is stronger than the Kimi baseline (68.0% versus 54.2%), the longer uninterrupted GPT exposure in the GPT-first archive is associated with the higher NTA result. GPT-first HMA instead allocates 51.1% to GPT and 46.3% to Kimi, whereas Kimi-first HMA still allocates 81.3% to Kimi and only 16.2% to GPT. These finite-budget differences accord with the startup effects in Appendix A.2; improvement from interruption remains conditional on continuation advantage (Theorem 3.5).

Model time allocation.

We reconstruct occupied model-session intervals from native session and controller logs over the first six hours. Native creation and completion records determine session endpoints. For an interrupted session without a completion record, we use the next session or option start, or the active attempt’s end, whichever occurs first. Intervals are intersected with active-runtime windows; pause gaps and auxiliary subagent sessions are excluded, and final review is attributed to its executing model. If wj(u)w_{j}^{(u)} is the resulting model-uu duration on task jj, its mean budget share is 100​∑j=175wj(u)/(75⋅21600)100\sum_{j=1}^{75}w_{j}^{(u)}/(75\cdot 21600). All returns to a model are accumulated. Unallocated time averages 0.07% and 0.15% for GPT-first and Kimi-first NTA, and 2.63% and 2.49% for the corresponding HMA runs. These shares include tool execution and waiting within sessions.

Recorded starting-order exceptions.

Workflow labels retain the archived nominal configurations. In the GPT-first NTA archive, seven of 75 tasks have Kimi as the earliest recorded native session; the other NTA configuration and both HMA runs match their nominal initial models on all 75 tasks. Runtime attribution follows the recorded model, and all tasks remain included. Thus the historical NTA groups are configuration comparisons rather than perfectly controlled starting-order interventions.

Designated-partner participation.

We measure participation from the first recorded response by the nominal second agent (Kimi in the GPT-first configuration and GPT in the Kimi-first configuration), excluding turn-review sessions. This measures observable access to search, rather than an exact controller launch time. Tasks with no such response are right-censored at six hours; counts retain all 75 tasks in the denominator. Table 10 reports these response-based timing statistics separately from the session-duration estimates above. With GPT first, the second agent’s mean within-task share of output tokens before hour 5.75 rises from 13.0% under NTA to 36.1% under HMA. A cap limits experiments per option; it does not impose a fixed wall-clock duration on an experiment.

F.2 Effects of the Fixed Interruption Cap

We hold GPT as the initial agent and compare executed HMA policies with k∈{1,3,5}k\in\{1,3,5\}, complementing the observed-prefix analysis in Appendix B.

Configurations and results.

Each cap contributes one repeat over 75 tasks with the same model pair, max reasoning effort, and nominal six-hour budget including final review. The k=1k=1 and k=3k=3 archives use a 21,700-second terminal window. Table 11 reports the final medal counts and rates, also plotted in Figure 7(b). These cap configurations and the reverse-order configuration are used for scheduling ablations; the main comparison retains its six configurations.

Empirical selection within the candidate range.

The prefix statistics in Appendix B motivate candidates 1≤k≤51\leq k\leq 5. Among the executed GPT-first runs, k=1,3,5k=1,3,5 yield 65.3%, 66.7%, and 70.7% medals, respectively, against the GPT goal mean of 68.0%. These results support selecting k=5k=5 within the tested finite caps for this order and horizon. Theorem 3.5 gives the corresponding conditional advantage criterion; the prefix statistics guide candidate selection without directly estimating its continuation values.

Interaction with time and starting order.

A larger cap permits longer uninterrupted experiment blocks before handoff, while the six-hour deadline limits the partner’s subsequent search. Given GPT’s stronger standalone performance, the GPT-first cap trend and higher GPT-first NTA result are consistent with a benefit from preserving more continuous GPT search. Conversely, k=5k=5 improves the Kimi-first result and reduces sensitivity to the initial agent. The limited horizon can therefore leave the pair’s complementary capabilities incompletely exploited, making cap size and initial-agent choice jointly relevant. The recorded starting-order exceptions in Appendix F.1 delimit this interpretation.

F.3 Natural Termination before the Cap

We report option-closure outcomes from terminal controller receipts and evaluator ledgers for the six main-table HMA configurations. One complete repeat per configuration, using the first Opus-first GPT repeat, yields 450 task runs with the same answer keys and final-candidate rule as Table 2.

Option closure.

Table 12 separates the first option from later options and distinguishes reaching five accepted experiments, natural termination before five, and closure at the exploration deadline. Final review sessions are excluded. Initial options contain 57 natural exits among 446 closures before the deadline (12.8%); later options contain 598 among 992 (60.3%). Across all options, 655/1,438 closures before the deadline are natural (45.5%). Of the 655 natural exits, 248 produce no accepted experiment. These are retained in the audit. One GPT–DeepSeek deadline receipt omits the cap field following a controller timeout; its accepted count is zero, and the recorded standing submission agrees with the adopted fallback. All 1,888 recorded option counts are at most five.

F.4 Final Review and Historical Any-Medal Retention

We evaluate retention of historically attained any-medal outcomes on the same 450 task runs as Appendix F.3, supplementing the mechanism in Section 3.4.

Selection-only comparison.

We hold each recorded exploration trajectory fixed and compare the returned candidate with the candidate standing immediately before final review. The reserved final review time is not reallocated to search, so this measures the effect of final selection rather than a rerun with a longer exploration budget.

Historical any-medal retention.

For each task run, historical any-medal status is one if any accepted exploration candidate earns bronze or better, and zero otherwise. We compute this status from offline evaluator records before final review; repeated receipts for a reviewed candidate add no new historical outcome. Historical any-medal retention is the fraction of historically medal-positive task runs whose selected candidate earns a medal. Table 13 compares this fraction before and after final review. Of 450 task runs, 330 produce a medal-winning candidate; final review raises retained medals from 311/330 (94.2%) to 319/330 (96.7%), recovering eight medals without losing any held immediately before final review.

Across all 450 runs, the returned candidate matches the historical any-medal status in 439 (97.6%), including 120 runs that never produce a medal. The conditional retention rate of 96.7% excludes these 120 runs. Final review changes 40 selections (8.9%); 311/319 final medals (97.5%) were already held before final review. Thirty-five GLM-pair final reviews are silent and one DeepSeek-pair final review fails; their recorded fallback candidates remain included. This audit measures historical any-medal retention at final selection.

Medal recovery and remaining misses.

On MBM-01 with GPT–DeepSeek-V4.1, the first GPT option reaches 0.84671 without a medal, and DeepSeek reaches bronze at 0.85445. The returning GPT replaces the standing result with 0.75795; final review restores the archived DeepSeek candidate and recovers the medal. On MBM-20 with GPT–GLM, GPT produces a gold-medal candidate at 0.84835, but the final GLM candidate scores 0.25403; final review restores 0.84835. In aggregate, final review reduces missed historical medals from 19 to 11, supporting its role in retaining search outcomes at final selection.

Appendix G Case Studies of Heterogeneous Alternation

We examine four model pairs across five model families: GPT–Opus, GPT–DeepSeek, GLM–Kimi, and DeepSeek–Kimi. The INGV case in Section 4.4 is followed by examples from text prediction, image regression, and satellite positioning.

Selection and measurement.

We selected task runs with inspectable artifacts, controller logs, evaluator receipts, and native response records. GPT–Opus, GPT–DeepSeek, and DeepSeek–Kimi occur in the main comparison; GLM–Kimi is an additional combination using the same k=5k=5 workflow. Following the trajectory analysis of Zhao et al. (2026), we align each accepted candidate with its producing option using controller counts and receipt times. Test scores are evaluated offline and were hidden from the agents; all accepted scores, including regressions, are plotted. Goal references use three runs per constituent. The appendix figures compare disjoint first- and last-20-response windows; options with fewer than 40 responses show their counts instead. Final review is excluded from token statistics and preserves the standing candidate in all four cases. Response renewal is compared within the same model, since tokenizers and policies differ. These cases illustrate observed mechanisms rather than estimating their average causal effect.

G.1 INGV Volcanic Eruption Prediction

Repeated refinement.

On INGV (MBH-07), GPT and Opus complete seven exploration options with 5, 5, 5, 2, 5, 1, and 4 accepted experiments and 77, 263, 251, 59, 110, 49, and 48 responses, respectively. Options 1, 2, 3, and 5 reach the cap; options 4 and 6 end naturally, and option 7 reaches the deadline. Their best MAEs are 1,123,915, 41,214, 39,061, 39,878, 37,422, 36,934, and 34,234: five of the six post-handoff options improve the historical best, while the fourth option regresses. Shared features and cached predictions support successive refinements. The trace records GPT reusing and pruning Opus’s retrieval features, Opus adding consistency constraints for paired windows, GPT introducing an uncertainty-based residual gate, Opus refining its calibration, and GPT enforcing joint temporal feasibility.

Score comparisons and plot conventions.

After the first Opus session reaches 41,214 MAE, subsequent alternation lowers it to 34,234, a further 16.9% improvement and 46.5% below the best of six constituent goal runs (63,991). Native MAE resolves progress beyond the already-gold goal results. Figure 5(a) retains all 27 accepted scores, including regressions, without smoothing; it uses a logarithmic axis with a linear inset for late options. Horizontal lines mark the gold threshold (3,971,366), the minimum MAE in MLE-bench’s 621-entry reference leaderboard (3,438,191), and the best constituent goal endpoint. Blue and purple regions identify GPT and Opus, and dotted vertical lines mark handoffs.

Response measurement and renewal.

In Figure 5(b), each point averages output tokens per response from the preceding accepted submission or option start to the current acceptance. The 27 intervals contain 826 responses, excluding 31 trailing responses; final review is excluded. Comparing the first experiment after each return with the same model’s preceding last experiment, mean response length increases on four of five returns by a factor of 1.6–3.6; the final Opus return has a ratio of 0.94.

G.2 Google QUEST Q&A Labeling: GPT–DeepSeek

Repeated reuse of text-model predictions.

On Google QUEST Q&A Labeling (MBM-10), GPT-5.6-sol and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash complete seven options, five of which produce 23 accepted candidates. GPT initializes sparse-text and encoder models; DeepSeek completes additional DeBERTa fits and combines their saved predictions. Subsequent sessions reuse these artifacts for target-specific blending, calibration, and larger-encoder refinement. The first five options achieve best Spearman correlations of 0.45664, 0.47124, 0.48741, 0.50381, and 0.50760. The returned candidate scores 0.50747, versus 0.47252 for the best of six constituent goal runs (Figure 8). At the first returns, GPT’s mean response length rises from 168.9 to 529.1 tokens and DeepSeek’s from 647.2 to 1060.9; GPT’s next return instead falls from 616.7 to 339.2. The final two options produce no accepted experiment, so neither response renewal nor useful progress occurs at every handoff.

G.3 PetFinder Pawpularity: GLM–Kimi

Extending a shared prediction pool.

On PetFinder Pawpularity (MBM-27), GLM-5.3 builds CLIP and DINOv2 feature caches, regressors, and calibrated predictions before Kimi K3 takes over at 2.40 hours. Kimi reuses the out-of-fold predictions in a constrained stack and adds concatenated-feature ridge and MLP members, improving the best test RMSE from 16.87437 to 16.78333. Returning GLM explores further combinations and reaches 16.77953; the returned candidate scores 16.85639 and earns gold (Figure 9). Neither constituent earns a medal in its three goal runs. The three productive options contain 5, 5, and 3 experiments; the final Kimi option adds none. GLM’s returning first 20 responses average 724.5 tokens, compared with 503.8 in its preceding option’s last 20. The final score regression remains visible: artifact reuse improves the search trajectory without ensuring that the returned candidate is its best.

G.4 Google Smartphone Decimeter: DeepSeek–Kimi

Late correction after an unsuccessful refinement.

On the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge 2022 (MBH-12), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash builds a GNSS fusion pipeline with Doppler constraints and robust optimization, reaching 4.33091 mean haversine error. Kimi K3 improves it to 4.28914, but DeepSeek’s next option leaves a worse candidate at 5.35529. Returning at 5.08 hours, Kimi retains the shared solver, checks the mean-error objective, and replaces straight-line extrapolation through an end-of-log outage with a direction-matched route from public training trajectories. Its accepted candidate reaches 2.77310 and earns bronze, a 42.1% reduction from the best of six constituent goal endpoints (4.78536), none of which earns a medal (Figure 10). Kimi’s first 20 returning responses average 847.9 tokens, below the preceding Kimi option’s last-20 mean of 1010.0. This late quality gain therefore does not require a response-length rebound.
